newsitem.title: MEXICO: Fall of top drug fighter embarrasses Mexico, U.S..
newsitem.headline: Fall of top drug fighter embarrasses Mexico, U.S..

text.p: The shocking dismissal of Mexico's top anti-drugs fighter on charges he took money from a powerful cocaine trafficker has embarrassed the U.S. and Mexican governments, which had praised him as an honest hero.

Mexican government officials scrambled on Wednesday to limit the damage a day after dismissing Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, 62, as head of the National Institute for Drug Control for being in the pay of Amado Carrillo Fuentes, reputedly the country's most powerful drug baron.
Gutierrez, who had been out of public view for two weeks, supposedly under treatment in a military hospital, was arrested and taken to the Almoloya maximum security jail outside Mexico City.
"Crimes do a lot of damage but the damage would be worse if there was an attempt to hide them for fear of a scandal," the Mexican presidency said in a statement on Wednesday.
A senior government source told Reuters Gutierrez had tipped off Carrillo Fuentes that the army was about to raid his sister's wedding last month, allowing him to escape.

"We have absolutely no doubt that he is a criminal, a very smart criminal," the source said. "He had two lifestyles, an austere monastic one shown to work colleagues and another sybaratic one with amazing mansions and a girlfriend."

When interrogated about a luxury apartment in which he lived in Mexico City, the general became nervous and gave conflicting answers, the source said. "Once we applied the lie detector, he really started to sink."

Mexican law enforcement officials have proved notoriously corrupt in the past -- one Mexico City police chief built a vast seaside villa in a mock Roman style with his ill-gotten gains -- but Gutierrez's fall was especially embarrassing because he was supposed to be different.

An army general with a long record of distinguished service, he was hailed as an incorruptible hero by Americans and Mexicans alike when he was appointed only two months ago. Officials pointed to his success in securing a string of arrests of top traffickers over the past few years while he headed an army division in the western state of Guadalajara.

Less than a month ago, on Jan. 24, Attorney-General Jorge Madrazo introduced Gutierrez to foreign correspondents as a distinguished official with a spotless record of honesty. And three weeks ago U.S. drug czar Gen. Barry McCaffrey praised him as an "honest man and no-nonsense" former army commander.

Referring to Gutierrez and Madrazo, McCaffrey told reporters on Jan. 29: "Let me tell you, up front, we are proud of our association with these two public servants." McCaffrey was travelling on Wednesday but his office released a terse statement describing Gutierrez' arrest as "appropriate".

"We are extremely disappointed that corruption may have reached such a level in Mexico," the statement said. "This demonstrates that Mexico is seriously threatened by corruption and violence but will take strong steps to root it out."

Gutierrez' fall was also a blow to a recent trend in Latin America of involving the military more closely in anti-drug operations, supposedly because soldiers were less corrupt than police in the region.

"Neither the greatest toughness, nor the strictest severity will be able to repair the damage which a bad high-ranking soldier inflicts on Mexico when he betrays all his values," Gen. Enrique Cervantes Aguirre said at a ceremony ironically Army Day.
